title: Electromagnetic Radiation and Matter
seo_title: EM Radiation Worksheets: Ionizing Radiation, UV, X-Rays and Health Claims (Physics)
standard_text: Evaluate the validity and reliability of claims in published materials of the effects that different frequencies of electromagnetic radiation have when absorbed by matter.
meta_desc: Free high school physics worksheets on electromagnetic radiation and matter (NGSS HS-PS4-4): ionizing and non-ionizing radiation, effects on the body, intensity and evaluating health claims. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: UV, X-rays and gamma rays can ionize atoms; radio and microwaves mainly heat or pass through.
body_html:
How to think about it

What radiation does depends on its frequency (photon energy).

  • Low frequency (radio, microwave, infrared, visible): non-ionizing; mostly heating or no effect.
  • High frequency (UV, X-rays, gamma): can ionize atoms and damage DNA.
  • Intensity falls as 1 ÷ distance². Judge claims by their source, data, controls and whether they show cause.
Example

100 W/m² at 1 m. At 2 m?

100 × (1 ÷ 2)²

Answer: 25 W/m²

Example

Microwaves or X-rays: more harmful per photon?

Higher frequency

Answer: X-rays

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all radiation causes cancer.
  • Thinking microwave ovens make food radioactive.
  • Thinking brighter light has higher-energy photons.

faq.q: What is the difference between ionizing and non-ionizing radiation?
faq.a: Ionizing radiation (X-rays, gamma rays, some UV) has enough photon energy to knock electrons off atoms. Non-ionizing radiation (radio, microwave, infrared, visible) does not.

faq.q: Are cell phones and microwaves dangerous?
faq.a: They use non-ionizing radiation. Microwaves heat food by making water molecules move faster; they do not make food radioactive.

faq.q: How do you judge a claim about radiation?
faq.a: Check who made it, whether there is data from controlled studies, whether others reviewed it, and whether it shows cause or only a correlation.
